# Interprofessional practice, referral and looking after yourself

> *A safe clinician is defined as much by what they refer as by what they do: good advice stays within
> the edges of the role, and a clean hand-off follows when a patient crosses them. The clinician's own
> health is the one instrument that cannot be referred out, and it needs looking after.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Distinguish universal nutrition advice, which any clinician gives, from medical nutrition therapy,
  which a registered dietitian delivers.
- Recognise the triggers for referral to a dietitian, and refer.
- Write a dietitian referral that carries what the dietitian needs to act on.
- Describe the roles in a nutrition care team, and explain why intensive trial results cannot be
  promised from brief advice.
- Explain why a clinician's own sleep, diet and activity matter for their health and their counselling.
- Describe how Healthier SG builds the advise-or-refer line into Singapore's primary care.
:::

## Interprofessional practice at a glance {#sec-overview}

Good dietary care calls for humility with competence: a clinician knows where their own role ends and
someone else's begins. Brief, general, evidence-aligned advice is every clinician's work, and
individualised therapy for a condition is a dietitian's. The care around a chronic condition is shared
by a team, which Singapore's health system is built to support. The clinician's own diet, sleep and
activity matter too, as a wellbeing issue and, plausibly, a credibility one.

## Scope of practice: advise or refer {#sec-scope}

### Where the clinician's role ends {#sec-role-limits}

**Scope of practice** is the care a clinician's role allows them to deliver and be accountable for. It
is set by role and accountability as well as by knowledge: knowing the science is not a licence to
deliver treatment [@aclm2022comp; @afn2021curriculum]. At this stage of training, a clinician's
nutrition care is brief, general, evidence-aligned and patient-centred. That care draws on the toolkit
of the *What a Healthy Diet Looks Like*, *Assessing Diet & Talking to Patients* and
*Behaviour-Change Counselling* chapters, and the toolkit stops short of individualised therapy for a
medical condition.

Graduates consistently report feeling under-prepared to counsel on nutrition [@crowley2019], and the
professional response to that gap is to recognise it and refer, without overreaching to cover it.
Referral is a competency and a safety behaviour, not an admission of failure.

### The line: advice versus therapy {#sec-advice-therapy}

Two kinds of "diet advice" sit on either side of a clean line, and holding that line is the core skill
here:

Universal advice (in scope)
: General guidance that is safe for almost anyone and that every clinician should give: My Healthy
  Plate, "cut the sugary drinks", "more vegetables, less refined rice", the dietary-pattern message
  [@hpbHealthyPlate].

Medical nutrition therapy (MNT; refer)
: An individualised, therapeutic nutrition plan for a medical condition, delivered by a registered
  dietitian: a structured cycle of assessment, diagnosis, intervention and monitoring, evidence-based
  and outcome-tracked [@ada2026standards].

For type 2 diabetes, dietitian-delivered MNT is associated with reductions in HbA1c (a marker of
average blood-glucose control) of roughly 0.3–2.0%, a guideline-reported range across trials of
differing intensity, not a guaranteed effect [@ada2026standards].

Conflating the two fails in both directions. Treat all advice as MNT and you freeze, too afraid to say
anything safe; treat MNT as ordinary advice and you overstep into care you can't be accountable for.

Run a few patients through the line below. The same question ("should I advise, or refer?") lands
differently depending on complexity.

<div data-island="advise-refer" data-src="/diagrams/advise-refer.yml"></div>

### Referral triggers {#sec-referral-triggers}

A short checklist catches most referral needs, so each case need not be judged from scratch. Refer to a
dietitian when there is:

- a complex condition, or several at once, such as type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease or
  cardiovascular disease (see the *Type 2 Diabetes*, *Chronic Kidney Disease* and
  *Cardiovascular Disease & Hypertension* chapters), or gastrointestinal disease;
- unintended weight loss or malnutrition risk (see the *Undernutrition & Malnutrition* chapter for
  screening);
- obesity needing structured management, or pregnancy or paediatric nutrition needs;
- a food allergy or intolerance, or any eating-disorder concern;
- advice needs that exceed general guidance, or a patient who is not progressing.

These are recognition triggers, not treatment cues: your job is to spot them and hand over, and the
dietitian works up the plan.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a clinician knows the dietary science of diabetes and kidney disease well. Why should she still refer a patient with both to a dietitian?
Scope of practice is set by role and accountability, so knowing the science is not a licence to
deliver treatment. An individualised therapeutic plan for a medical condition is medical nutrition
therapy, delivered by a registered dietitian, and a complex or multiple condition is a referral
trigger. Writing that plan herself would overstep into care she cannot be accountable for.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does treating every piece of diet advice as medical nutrition therapy also fail patients?
Universal advice, such as My Healthy Plate or cutting sugary drinks, is safe for almost anyone, and
every clinician should give it. A clinician who treats all advice as therapy freezes and says nothing
safe, so the patient loses help that was within scope. Conflating advice and therapy fails in both
directions: overstepping on one side, silence on the other.
:::

## Referring, and working as a team {#sec-referral-team}

### Writing a referral that helps {#sec-referral-letter}

A referral is only as useful as its contents, and a vague one wastes a scarce resource. "Please advise
on diet" tells the dietitian nothing. A referral that helps carries:

::: {.callout-note}
## What a good dietitian referral contains
- The reason for referral and its urgency.
- Relevant diagnoses, and how recent they are.
- Current medications.
- Key results, such as HbA1c, lipids and renal function (estimated glomerular filtration rate, eGFR).
- Weight or BMI, and the recent trend (gaining, stable, losing).
- The patient's goals and social context: who cooks, whether they eat out, whether they live alone.
:::

Completeness is itself a clinical skill: it turns a hand-off into a head start.

### The nutrition care team {#sec-care-team}

Nutrition care for a patient with a chronic condition is shared by a team, each member with a distinct
hand-off:

- the family doctor coordinates;
- the registered dietitian delivers MNT;
- the nurse monitors and educates;
- the pharmacist reviews medications;
- allied-health and community partners extend care beyond the clinic.

Team-based care is associated with better chronic-disease outcomes, since the whole is more than any
one professional's slice [@aclm2022comp; @afn2021curriculum].

That "more than one slice" cuts both ways: it is a common trap to over-claim the nutrition part of the
team's results. The headline lifestyle results (see the *Type 2 Diabetes* chapter) came from team-delivered, intensive programmes, not a clinic chat: remission in the DiRECT trial (Diabetes Remission Clinical Trial) ran on a structured total-diet-replacement programme in selected patients, who had early type 2 diabetes and were not on insulin [@lean2018direct], and the Diabetes Prevention Program reached its prevention effect with a 16-session curriculum [@dpp2002]. In total diet replacement, low-calorie formula meals replace ordinary food for a period.

Don't promise those outcomes from advice alone. The trial patients were selected, so check whether a
result applies to the patient in front of you (see the *Evidence vs Hype* chapter). The dose was
intensive, and a single clinic visit does not deliver it (see the *Behaviour-Change Counselling*
chapter).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a referral reads only "please advise on diet". Why does it waste a scarce resource?
A referral is only as useful as its contents. Medical nutrition therapy is individualised, so the
dietitian needs the reason and urgency, the diagnoses, medications, key results, the weight trend, and
the patient's goals and social context; a vague note supplies none of them. A complete referral spends
the dietitian's time well and turns the hand-off into a head start.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has read that a diet put diabetes into remission. Why can't a clinic conversation promise her the same result?
The headline results came from team-delivered, intensive programmes. DiRECT's remission used a
structured total-diet-replacement programme in selected patients with early type 2 diabetes not on
insulin, and the Diabetes Prevention Program's effect came from a 16-session curriculum. Brief advice
from one clinician is a different dose, often given to a different patient, so it cannot claim those
outcomes.
:::

## The clinician's own health: physician, mind thyself {#sec-clinician-health}

The last part of the role is the one clinicians skip: their own health. Clinicians who look after their
own diet and activity are observed to counsel more often, and arguably more credibly. The evidence is
associational, not proof of cause, but it is consistent [@lobelo2015rolemodel; @lianov2010].

A clinician's own habits matter for more than role-modelling. Short sleep shifts the appetite hormones
(see the *Appetite & Weight Regulation* chapter), raising ghrelin, blunting satiety and pushing intake
up [@sleepRestriction]. The packed-roster diet of skipped meals, *kopi* and five hours' sleep therefore
works against the clinician's own metabolic health. The remedy is a sustainable micro-plan rather than
an overhaul: one realistic food swap, a sleep anchor (a fixed bedtime or wake time) and a short daily
walk. Practitioner wellbeing is a professional and patient-safety issue, not an indulgence, and guarding
against burnout is a longitudinal skill to keep working at [@lianov2010].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a junior doctor on a packed roster sleeps five hours a night and skips meals. Why does that matter for her own health, as well as for how she counsels?
Short sleep shifts the appetite hormones: ghrelin rises, satiety is blunted and intake goes up, so
skipped meals, *kopi* and short sleep work against her own metabolic health. Her habits also bear on
her patients, because clinicians who look after their own diet and activity are observed to counsel
more often, although that evidence is associational. The remedy is a sustainable micro-plan (one food
swap, a sleep anchor, a short daily walk), not an overhaul.
:::

## The Singapore picture: Healthier SG {#sec-singapore}

Singapore has built the scaffold that makes referral and follow-up happen. Healthier SG is the national shift toward proactive, relationship-based prevention in primary care (see the *Why Nutrition Matters* chapter). Since its national roll-out in 2023, Healthier SG has given each enrolled resident one family doctor, who
co-develops with them a personalised **Health Plan**, the natural place to raise a nutrition concern
and refer it [@mohHealthierSG].

The model is team-based and community-linked. Family doctors can make **social prescriptions**
(referrals to community programmes such as Health Promotion Board activities, Active Ageing Centres and
SportSG), and a **tiered dietitian pathway** has clinicians give first-line dietary advice and escalate
complex cases to a registered dietitian [@mohEatWiseSG]. The line between advising and referring is
therefore built into the health system itself.

Funding follows the same logic. The **Healthier SG Chronic Tier** (from 2024) is the subsidy framework
that keeps chronic-disease follow-up affordable: enrolled holders of Community Health Assist Scheme
(CHAS), Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation cards receive means-tested subsidies of up to about
87.5% on selected chronic medications, with no dollar cap, plus up to about \$360 a year toward other
care components such as consultations and tests [@mohChronicTier].

![Healthier SG puts an enrolled family doctor at the centre of a team-and-community model: a shared Health Plan, hand-offs to the dietitian, nurse and pharmacist, social prescribing to community partners, and Chronic Tier subsidies that keep follow-up affordable.](/figures/mechanisms/hsg-ecosystem.svg){#fig-hsg-ecosystem}

The published Chronic Tier scheme centres on medications and care components and does not spell out a
dedicated dietitian or MNT subsidy line. Dietitian and allied-health access typically flows through
polyclinic, specialist and cluster services, and the exact funding evolves. Explain the referral pathway
and the advise-or-refer principle to patients, and check current figures before quoting them.

## Where does a clinician's role end? {#sec-close}

A clinician's role ends at the edge of what they can safely be accountable for, not at the edge of what
they know. In nutrition care that edge is the line between universal advice and medical nutrition
therapy, and where a patient falls depends on their complexity. A well adult asking how to eat more
healthily, or whether to swap white rice for brown, sits well inside the role, because universal advice
is every clinician's job. A patient with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, early kidney impairment and
three medicines sits beyond it, because her plan has to be individualised medical nutrition therapy.
Beyond the edge, the clinician still has a part: a complete referral, and safe universal advice while
the patient waits.
